cards.explanation: The answer is to test how they live and turn back to God. The writer says, “Let us examine and test our ways, and turn back to the LORD.” Look at that word "us," friends. He doesn't point at the crowd from the outside. He stands in the line with everybody else, and I love him for it. (Lam 3:40)

The answer is "sinned." The prayer says, “We have sinned and rebelled; You have not forgiven.” Nobody in that line makes an excuse, friends. I've blamed a cookie sheet for a scorched batch before, but this prayer doesn't blame a thing, just plain honest words. (Lam 3:42)

The answer is False. The prayer says, “We have sinned and rebelled; You have not forgiven.” They don't tell God He has already forgiven them, friends. They say the hard part straight, with nothing sugarcoated. (Lam 3:42)

The answer is any prayer. The writer says, “You have covered Yourself with a cloud that no prayer can pass through.” That's how he describes it to God. And look at what he does anyway, friends: he keeps on speaking to God, right to the end of the passage. (Lam 3:44)

The answer is scum and refuse. The writer says, “You have made us scum and refuse among the nations.” Ouch. I think those words hurt to write, and he says them anyway. He's honest about how low it got. (Lam 3:45)
The answer is False. The writer says, “All our enemies open their mouths against us.” These foes aren't quiet, friends. Their mouths are open against his people. (Lam 3:46)

The answer is until the LORD looks down and sees. The writer says his eyes overflow “…until the LORD looks down from heaven and sees.” So the tears have an end in view, friends, and it's the LORD seeing. I think that tells you where the writer is looking while he cries. (Lam 3:49–50)

The answer is True, and that's the verse word for word: “My eyes bring grief to my soul because of all the daughters of my city.” His grief is tied to the daughters of his city. I think this man carries his whole city with him, friends. (Lam 3:51)

The answer is a pit. The writer says, “They dropped me alive into a pit and cast stones upon me.” I think this one hurts, friends. He says it plainly, and that's how we know how deep it went. (Lam 3:53)

The answer is "die." The writer says, “…I thought I was going to die.” The waters were over his head, and he says what he thought. I think that's about as low as a man can get, friends, and he's honest about it. (Lam 3:54)

The answer is that he calls on the LORD's name. The writer says, “I called on Your name, O LORD, out of the depths of the Pit.” He calls from the depths of the Pit, right where he is. That's the part I'd bake into a plaque, friends. (Lam 3:55)

The answer is "Do not be afraid." The writer says the LORD drew near when he called, and said, “Do not be afraid.” Think about the order, friends. He called first, and the LORD came close. I think that's one of the sweetest lines in the passage. (Lam 3:57)

The answer is True. The writer says, “You defend my cause, O Lord; You redeem my life.” Notice how the verse sits right after the LORD drew near, friends. His words here are about what the Lord does. (Lam 3:57–58)

The answer is True. The writer says, “You have seen, O LORD, the wrong done to me; vindicate my cause!” First he says what the LORD has seen. Then he asks. It's all one breath, friends, and I like how plain it is. (Lam 3:59)

The answer is in song. The writer says, “…see how they mock me in song.” I bet a tune that's about you is the hardest kind to get out of your head, friends. It's a rough thing to live with. (Lam 3:63)

The answer is False. The writer says, “You will pay them back what they deserve, O LORD, according to the work of their hands.” Going free isn't in his words, friends. He says the LORD will pay them back. (Lam 3:64)

The answer is False. Verse 43 says, “You have covered Yourself in anger and pursued us…” The very last verse says, “You will pursue them in anger and exterminate them from under Your heavens, O LORD.” The word turned from "us" to "them," friends. His enemies are now the ones pursued. (Lam 3:43, 66)
